title: A Wall Street 'Sex Slave' Scandal Has Turned Into a Defamation War — and a Nepali American Banker Is at the Centre of It
excerpt: JPMorgan executive Lorna Hajdini has filed a countersuit against former colleague Chirayu Rana, calling his explosive sexual-assault allegations 'entirely fabricated.' The case is reverberating through South Asian professional circles.
body:
When a bombshell lawsuit hit New York State court earlier this month accusing a JPMorgan Chase executive of turning a junior colleague into a "sex slave," Wall Street braced for another reckoning. Within days, the story had gone viral — not least because the plaintiff, initially filed as "John Doe," turned out to be Chirayu Rana, a 35-year-old Nepali American former senior vice president in the bank's leveraged finance division.

Now Lorna Hajdini, the JPMorgan executive director named in the suit, has fired back with a defamation countersuit, calling Rana's claims "false and malicious" and accusing him of orchestrating a months-long smear campaign to destroy her career and reputation.

## The Original Allegations

Rana's complaint, filed under a pseudonym before his identity was revealed by media reports, painted a lurid picture of workplace abuse. He alleged that Hajdini — his direct superior — sexually assaulted him, spiked his drinks with Viagra-like and date-rape drugs, repeatedly groped him, and bombarded him with unwanted sexual advances over several months in 2024. The suit claimed she once fondled him under the table during a meeting with a potential client while whispering about a threesome.

According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal, JPMorgan had offered Rana a $1 million settlement before the allegations became public. Rana rejected the offer and reportedly countered with a $20 million demand, according to the New York Post. The bank says an internal investigation found no evidence supporting his claims and that Rana declined to fully cooperate with parts of the review process.

## Hajdini's Counterattack

Through her lawyers, Hajdini has categorically denied every allegation. "She never dated this individual, never had a sexual or romantic encounter with him of any kind, and never gave him any drugs," her legal team stated. JPMorgan has backed her position, calling the original complaint "completely fabricated."

The defamation suit, filed on May 19, seeks to hold Rana accountable for what Hajdini describes as calculated reputational damage. Her attorneys argue that the lawsuit was designed to extract a massive payout and that Rana's claims were crafted for viral social media consumption rather than legal merit.

## The South Asian Dimension

The case has generated intense discussion within Nepali American and broader South Asian professional circles in the United States. The original lawsuit included allegations of racial harassment tied to Rana's Nepalese background — claims that struck a nerve in diaspora communities where workplace discrimination in elite financial institutions remains a persistent concern.

Online debate has been fierce and divided. Some in the community view Rana as a whistleblower exposing the kind of power abuse that male employees rarely report. Others point to JPMorgan's internal findings and Hajdini's vigorous denial as reasons for caution. AI-generated videos and viral commentary have amplified the story far beyond financial media, making it one of the most discussed Wall Street controversies in recent memory.

Rana, who left JPMorgan and briefly worked at investment firm Bregal Sagemount, has since departed that role as well. The firm confirmed it had no prior knowledge of the allegations during his employment.

## What's Next

The legal battle is far from over. Rana's original complaint was briefly pulled from court records for "corrections" before being refiled with two sworn witness affidavits from redacted names who claim they saw inappropriate conduct. Further hearings are expected in the coming weeks. The defamation countersuit adds a new layer of complexity to a case that has already consumed Wall Street gossip channels and South Asian community forums alike.

For the diaspora professional community watching from trading desks, tech offices, and medical practices across the United States, the outcome matters beyond the two individuals involved. It will test how seriously corporate America takes internal complaints from employees of colour, how the legal system handles duelling narratives of abuse and fabrication, and whether the viral attention cycle has made it harder — or easier — to pursue genuine workplace grievances.

Daniel Kaiser, the attorney representing Rana and a partner known for representing accusers in the Jeffrey Epstein case, has signalled his client intends to fight. JPMorgan's legal team appears equally resolute. In this particular Wall Street drama, the only certainty is that nothing will be settled quietly.
